messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj, a 41-year-old South Asian park ranger in a committed relationship, has been struggling with the aftermath of his captivity experience for years. The trauma has left him with vivid and painful memories that frequently intrude into his daily life. The traumatic event occurred several years ago when Raj was captured by hostile forces during a routine patrol. Held captive for weeks, he endured humiliation, physical pain, and isolation from others. During this time, the sense of being completely under someone else's control became deeply embedded in his psyche. The fear and helplessness he felt were overwhelming. Since then, any mention of military topics or seeing people in uniform triggers flashbacks that transport Raj back to those terrifying moments. He vividly remembers a few snapshots from his captivity: the cold floor, the harsh lighting, and the feeling of being confined. These memories are so intense that when he experiences them, it feels as if the event is happening all over again. This re-experiencing causes him significant distress and physical pain in the same parts of his body where he was hurt during captivity. Raj has also developed a deep-seated belief that he cannot trust safety even when others reassure him. He finds it impossible to shake off the feeling that danger lurks around every corner, especially when he is startled by unexpected movements nearby. These startle reactions are frequent and often cause him to freeze or react aggressively as if he were still in imminent danger. The memory of his captivity has also led Raj to adopt maladaptive strategies as a means of coping. He strictly controls what and how much he eats, believing that having control over something tangible like food helps alleviate the overwhelming sense of powerlessness from his trauma. Additionally, he often fantasizes about exacting revenge on those responsible for his suffering, which provides him with a fleeting sense of empowerment but only exacerbates his feelings of isolation and humiliation. Raj’s tendency to please others stems from an underlying fear that if he doesn’t go along with what they want, he will be abandoned or further humiliated. This people-pleasing behavior is another way he tries to regain control and feel safe in a world he now perceives as threatening. The narrative of his captivity and the subsequent negative appraisals have reinforced each other, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. His belief that he feels isolated and set apart from others leads him to withdraw further, which then triggers more intense memories of his isolation during captivity. Similarly, the humiliation he associates with the event makes it harder for him to trust safety or authority figures, who remind him of those who inflicted harm. Over time, Raj has noticed that his relationships have suffered. His partner finds it challenging to understand why he reacts so strongly to seemingly minor triggers like discussions about military topics or seeing someone in uniform. At work, he avoids patrolling areas where there might be people in uniforms, which has led to tension with his colleagues and supervisors. What finally brought Raj to seek help is the realization that these coping mechanisms are not working anymore; they only serve to reinforce his negative beliefs and memories. He is most afraid of being trapped by these recurring thoughts and feelings but also hopes for a way to break free from this cycle and regain control over his life.
